items.title: 3.1.2 Finding Maximum and Minimum Values of Quadratic Functions by Completing Square

blocks.text: Completing the square is a technique used to rewrite a quadratic function in the following vertex form:

blocks.text_alt: f of x equals a times (x minus h) squared plus k
h equals minus b over 2 a, and k equals c minus b squared over 4 a

items: If \(a > 0\), the minimum value of \(f(x)\) at \(x = h\) is \(k\).
If \(a < 0\), the maximum value of \(f(x)\) at \(x = h\) is \(k\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where do \(h\) and \(k\) come from? Complete the square on \(ax^{2} + bx + c\):
\[ax^{2} + bx + c\]
\[= a\left(x^{2} + \dfrac{b}{a}x\right) + c\]
\[= a\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} - \dfrac{b^{2}}{4a} + c\]
Comparing with \(a(x - h)^{2} + k\): \(h = -\frac{b}{2a}\) and \(k = c - \frac{b^{2}}{4a}\).
(In the middle step we add and subtract \(\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2}\) inside the bracket; multiplied by \(a\) it gives \(\frac{b^{2}}{4a}\).)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(k\) the smallest or largest value? A square is never negative: \((x - h)^{2} \ge 0\), and it equals 0 only at \(x = h\).
If \(a > 0\), then \(a(x - h)^{2} \ge 0\), so \(f(x) = a(x - h)^{2} + k \ge k\): the smallest value is \(k\), at \(x = h\).
If \(a < 0\), then \(a(x - h)^{2} \le 0\), so \(f(x) \le k\): the largest value is \(k\), at \(x = h\).
Note that \(k = f(h)\) as well, so you can also find \(k\) by substituting \(h\) into the function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The recipe for completing the square on \(ax^{2} + bx + c\):
1. Take \(a\) out of the \(x^{2}\) and \(x\) terms only.
2. Inside the bracket, add and subtract \(\left(\frac{\text{coefficient of } x}{2}\right)^{2}\).
3. Write the first three terms as a perfect square.
4. Multiply out the leftover number by \(a\) and combine it with \(c\).
Remember the difference: the maximum or minimum value is \(k\) (a \(y\)-value); it occurs at \(x = h\).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem: Find the maximum or minimum value of \(f(x) = -2x^{2} + 4x + 3\) by completing square.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = -2x^{2} + 4x + 3\), so \(a = -2\).
To find: the maximum or minimum value, and where it occurs.
Method: rewrite \(f(x)\) in vertex form \(a(x - h)^{2} + k\) by completing the square; then the sign of \(a\) tells us whether \(k\) is a maximum or a minimum.

Step 1: Take \(a\) out of the \(x\)-terms
\[f(x) = -2(x^{2} - 2x) + 3\]
Why: completing the square works when \(x^{2}\) has coefficient 1. Only the \(x^{2}\) and \(x\) terms go into the bracket: \(-2x^{2} + 4x = -2(x^{2} - 2x)\).

Step 2: Add and subtract the square of half the coefficient of \(x\)
\[f(x) = -2(x^{2} - 2x + 1 - 1) + 3\]
Why: half of \(-2\) is \(-1\), and \((-1)^{2} = 1\). Adding \(1\) and subtracting \(1\) changes nothing, but it makes the perfect square \(x^{2} - 2x + 1\).

Step 3: Write the perfect square
\[f(x) = -2[(x - 1)^{2} - 1] + 3\]
Why: \(x^{2} - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^{2}\).

Step 4: Open the square bracket and simplify
\[f(x) = -2(x - 1)^{2} + 2 + 3\]
\[f(x) = -2(x - 1)^{2} + 5\]
Why: \(-2 \times (-1) = +2\). Now the function is in vertex form with \(h = 1\), \(k = 5\).

Step 5: Decide maximum or minimum
Here \(a = -2 < 0\).
Therefore, the maximum value is 5, which occurs when \(x = 1\).
Why: \(-2(x - 1)^{2}\) is never positive, so \(f(x) \le 5\), with equality only at \(x = 1\).
blocks.answer: \(f(x) = -2(x - 1)^{2} + 5\). The maximum value is \(5\), which occurs when \(x = 1\).

Dots mark its highest point (1, 5), labelled Maximum value, the y-intercept (0, 3) and the x-intercepts near minus 0.58 and 2.58; a dashed line drops from (1, 5) to the x-axis.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's graph prints the \(y\)-axis number below the \(x\)-axis at \(-2\) as "2". It lies below the \(x\)-axis, so it is \(-2\), as in our figure.

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem: Find the maximum or minimum value of \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2x - 3\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{2} - 2x - 3\).
To find: the maximum or minimum value.
Method: here the book uses the vertex formulas \(h = -\frac{b}{2a}\) and \(k = c - \frac{b^{2}}{4a}\) directly; they are the result of completing the square.

Step 1: Read the coefficients
Here \(a = 1\), \(b = -2\), \(c = -3\).
Why: compare with \(ax^{2} + bx + c\), keeping each sign with its number.

Step 2: Find \(h\)
\[h = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{(-2)}{2(1)}\]
\[h = 1\]
Why: \(h\) is the \(x\)-value where the maximum or minimum occurs.

Step 3: Find \(k\)
\[k = c - \dfrac{b^{2}}{4a}\]
\[= -3 - \dfrac{(-2)^{2}}{4(1)}\]
\[= -3 - 1 = -4\]
Why: \(k\) is the maximum or minimum value itself. Note \((-2)^{2} = 4\), positive.

Step 4: Decide maximum or minimum
Here \(a = 1 > 0\).
Therefore, the minimum value of \(f(x)\) at \(x = 1\) is \(-4\).
Why: for \(a > 0\) the parabola opens upward, so the vertex is its lowest point.

Check:
\[f(1) = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4\]
Completing the square: \(x^{2} - 2x - 3 = (x - 1)^{2} - 1 - 3 = (x - 1)^{2} - 4\), which gives the same \(h = 1\), \(k = -4\).
blocks.answer: The minimum value of \(f(x)\) is \(-4\), at \(x = 1\).

blocks.alt: Graph of f(x) = x squared minus 2x minus 3 on a grid, x from minus 3 to 4 and y from minus 5 to 5. The parabola opens upward; its lowest point (1, minus 4) is marked, with a dashed line up to the x-axis at x = 1 and the note Minimum value occurs at x = 1.
blocks.caption: Figure: f(x) = x² − 2x − 3 has its minimum value −4 at x = 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Vertex form: \(f(x) = a(x - h)^{2} + k\), vertex \((h, k)\).
2. \(h = -\frac{b}{2a}\), \(k = c - \frac{b^{2}}{4a}\) (also \(k = f(h)\)).
3. \(a > 0\): minimum value \(k\) at \(x = h\). \(a < 0\): maximum value \(k\) at \(x = h\).
4. The reason: \((x - h)^{2} \ge 0\) for every real \(x\).
5. Check the answer by finding \(f(h)\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting to multiply the subtracted number by \(a\): in \(-2[(x - 1)^{2} - 1] + 3\) the \(-1\) becomes \(+2\), not \(-1\).
2. Reading \(h\) with the wrong sign: \((x - 1)^{2}\) gives \(h = 1\); \((x + 3)^{2}\) gives \(h = -3\).
3. Giving \(x = h\) as "the maximum value": the value is \(k\); \(h\) only tells where it occurs.
4. Calling \(k\) a minimum when \(a < 0\): always look at the sign of \(a\) first.
